chunks: Sa'd ibn 'Abdillah narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from 'Aban ibn 'Uthman, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who begins the recitation in prayer: does he recite 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful'? He said: 'Yes, if he begins the prayer, let him say it at the beginning of what he begins, and then what follows that is sufficient for him.'
And to add clarification to it, what he narrated:

key_terms.أَوَّلِ مَا يَفْتَتِحُ: the beginning of what he begins
key_terms.بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on reciting Bismillah at the start of prayer in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the legal status of reciting 'Bismillah' as a distinct act at the onset of prayer, distinguishing it from the continuous recitation of Surah al-Fatiha. This ruling highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the ritual propriety of invoking God's name before commencing the primary recitation, ensuring the prayer begins with explicit divine attribution. The hadith underscores the principle that once the initial invocation is made, it suffices for the subsequent verses, streamlining the ritual while maintaining spiritual focus.
